intro: Every long story is heading somewhere. In this last unit you read how Michael Heiser understood the ending of the Bible's story. He read it as a family story. God has a heavenly family and a human family. Both had rebels. In Heiser's reading, the story ends with the two families restored together, the nations won back, and God dwelling with his people in a renewed Eden.

You will read the texts he built on: John 1 and 10, Romans 8, Galatians 4, 1 Corinthians 6, Psalm 82, Isaiah 14, and Revelation 16 and 20–22. You will weigh his boldest proposals, such as his reading of Har Magedon as the mount of assembly. Beside each one you will meet other readings: human judges in Psalm 82, Israel at Sinai in rabbinic writings, Eastern Orthodox theosis, Jewish readings of God's children, and four ways to read Revelation.

By the end you will be able to explain what Heiser argued about believers' destiny and why he said they never become equal to God. You will be able to trace a word from Hebrew into Greek, compare a symbol with its Hebrew Bible source, and describe a debate fairly without taking a side.
bigQuestion: How did Heiser read the end of the Bible's story, from God's family restored to the nations healed, and how do other readers understand the same texts?

chapters.title: Believers as God's Family

story.title: Is It Not Written, Ye Are Gods?
story.kicker: A student reading John 10 for a class finds Jesus quoting a psalm that calls someone gods, and she has to find out why.
paragraphs: Rosa had a simple assignment for her senior seminar: read John chapter 10 and write one question about it. She expected the shepherd verses. She had heard those before. Then, near the end of the chapter, she stopped. In the King James Version, Jesus answers a crowd with a question of his own: 'Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?' She read it three times.

The footnote pointed her to Psalm 82:6. She opened the psalm. It was only eight verses long. God stands in a gathering and judges beings the psalm calls gods. Then comes the line Jesus quoted: 'I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.' The next verse says they will die like men. Rosa wrote in her margin: Who are these gods, and why would Jesus bring them up?

Her teacher, Mr. Okafor, did not give her one answer. He gave her three. Many older Christian commentators read the gods as human judges. Some rabbinic writings connect the verse with Israel receiving the Torah at Sinai. And Michael Heiser, a scholar of Hebrew and the ancient world, read Psalm 82 as a scene in God's heavenly council, the divine council, with real heavenly beings on trial.

Heiser went further. He argued that the whole Bible tells one long story about God's family. God has a heavenly family and a human family. Both were meant to live with him. Both had rebels. In Heiser's reading, the story ends with the two families restored together, and the people the New Testament calls children of God taking a place in that family.

Rosa changed her question. It was no longer only about John 10. It was now: What does the Bible say believers will become, and how do different readers keep that from sounding like people turning into God? This chapter follows her question through the texts.
story.think: Why might a teacher give three readings of a hard verse instead of one? What does a reader gain by hearing them side by side?

lessons.title: Two Families, One Household
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the Bible as the story of God's two families, heavenly and human, and argued that its goal is to bring them back together in one household.
reading: Job 38:7 describes the morning the earth was founded. The *sons of God* shouted for joy, the text says, while the morning stars sang together. The scene has an audience before any human appears. Heiser pointed to verses like this one to show that the Hebrew Bible pictures God already surrounded by heavenly beings when creation begins. He called this group God's heavenly family, and he connected it to the *divine council*, the gathering of heavenly beings around God's throne.

Then Genesis 1:26–27 has God make humans in his image. Heiser argued in The Unseen Realm (2015) that 'image' names a role more than a shape: humans were made to represent God on earth, the way the heavenly beings served him in the unseen realm. Eden, in his reading, was the place where the two families met. God, his heavenly household and his human household shared one home.

Both families had rebels in Heiser's reading: the serpent in Eden, the sons of God in Genesis 6, and the gods over the nations after Babel. So the story's goal, as he described it, is a *restoration*. God does not scrap the plan. He brings a human family back into his household and removes the rebels who ruled in his place. Heiser's summary is a family story, not a courtroom or a battle story first. Other scholars describe the Bible's big story with different themes, such as covenant, kingdom or salvation history, and many see these as overlapping.

words.d: a Hebrew Bible phrase for heavenly beings who serve God, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7
the scholarly term for the gathering of heavenly beings around God in texts like Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22
bringing something back to the condition or purpose it was meant to have

look.title: Two Households at Creation

lessons.title: The Nations Given Away
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8–9 as God handing the nations over to lesser heavenly beings after Babel, which sets up the Bible's promise to win them back.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 says that when the Most High divided the nations, he set their borders by a number. In the *Masoretic Text*, the standard medieval Hebrew text, the number matches the 'sons of Israel.' In a Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy found at Qumran, and in the *Septuagint*, the old Greek translation, the reading points instead to the 'sons of God.' Most modern text critics favor the older 'sons of God' reading, and several modern English translations follow it.

Heiser built a large part of his work on this verse. He connected it to Babel in Genesis 11. In his reading, when the nations rebelled at Babel, God gave them over to heavenly sons of God and kept Israel as his own portion (Deuteronomy 32:9). Those heavenly rulers later went bad, and Psalm 82 shows God judging them. Heiser called the nations 'disinherited,' meaning they had been handed away from God's direct care.

This matters for the story's ending. If the nations were given away, then the goal of the story includes winning them back. Heiser read Genesis 12:3, where all families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham, as the first hint of that plan. Readers who follow the Masoretic reading usually see Deuteronomy 32:8 as a statement about Israel's place among the peoples, without heavenly rulers over them.

the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Egypt in the third century BCE
Heiser's term for the peoples God handed over to lesser heavenly rulers after Babel

lessons.title: The Rebels Replaced
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that in the story's ending, faithful humans take up the places of rule once held by rebellious heavenly beings.
reading: Psalm 82:7 ends the trial of the gods with a verdict: they will die like men and fall like one of the princes. Heiser read this as a sentence on the heavenly rulers of the nations. They had judged unjustly (Psalm 82:2–4), so they would lose their posts. Psalm 82:8 then asks God himself to rise and judge the earth, 'for thou shalt inherit all nations' in the King James Version. Heiser saw the last verse as a promise that God would take the nations back.

Who would rule with God after that? Heiser pointed to Daniel 7. There, 'one like the Son of man' receives a kingdom from the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13–14). Later in the chapter the kingdom is given to 'the saints of the most High' (Daniel 7:18, 27). Heiser read this as God's people sharing the rule that the rebels lost. Scholars debate whether the 'saints' in Daniel 7 are humans, angels, or both, and Heiser knew the debate.

Heiser's word for this change was *displacement*: faithful humans displacing the fallen gods of the nations. He did not picture humans becoming the same kind of being as God. He pictured them being raised to a place of honor in God's council, as a new family around the same throne. Other readers describe the same passages as God's kingdom coming through Israel's Messiah, without stressing heavenly rulers being replaced.

words.d: Heiser's term for faithful humans taking over the places of rule once held by rebellious heavenly beings
the title for God seated on the throne in the vision of Daniel 7
the holy ones who receive the kingdom in Daniel 7:18 and 7:27; readers debate whether they are human, heavenly or both

look.title: From Verdict to Kingdom

lessons.title: Power to Become Sons of God
lessons.mainIdea: John 1:12 says that those who received Jesus were given the right to become children of God, born of God rather than of human descent.
reading: The Gospel of John opens with a poem about the Word. Near its end comes John 1:12. The King James Version says that to those who received him, 'gave he power to become the sons of God.' The Greek word behind 'power' is *exousia*, which also means right or authority. Many modern translations say 'the right to become children of God.' Verse 13 adds that they are born 'not of blood' or human will, 'but of God.'

Heiser noticed that the phrase 'sons of God' in the Hebrew Bible usually named heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7. In the New Testament the same family language is used for people who trust in Jesus. For Heiser this was no accident. He read it as the human family being brought into the same household as God's heavenly family, which fits his picture of the story's goal.

Other readers stress different things in the verse. Many Christian interpreters focus on the new birth: becoming God's child is a gift received by faith, not something earned or inherited. Some scholars point out that John's Gospel often contrasts birth 'from above' with ordinary birth, as in John 3:3–7. Both readings agree on the plain words: the verse names a new family status that comes from God.

words.d: a Greek word meaning power, right or authority; used in John 1:12
the English for the Greek logos in John 1:1–14, a title John gives to the one who became flesh
being born 'from above' or 'of God,' language found in John 1:13 and John 3:3–7

check.q: According to John 1:13, how are these children born?

check.why: John 1:13 says they are born not of blood or human will, but of God.

check.q: Why did Heiser find the phrase 'sons of God' in John 1:12 important?

Because the Hebrew Bible used it for heavenly beings, and here it is used for people
Because John wrote it in Hebrew
Because it proves the Watchers were human

lessons.title: Adoption in Romans 8
lessons.mainIdea: Romans 8:14–23 calls believers adopted children of God and pictures all creation waiting for them to be revealed.
reading: Paul wrote Romans around 57 CE to believers in the city of Rome. In Romans 8:14 he says that those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. In verse 15 he says they have received 'the Spirit of *adoption*,' by which they cry 'Abba, Father.' *Abba* is an Aramaic word for father that Jesus himself uses in prayer in Mark 14:36. Paul keeps an Aramaic word inside a Greek letter, which shows how important the family word was to early believers.

Then Paul widens the picture. In Romans 8:19 the whole creation waits eagerly for 'the manifestation of the sons of God,' meaning the moment they are revealed. Verse 22 says creation groans like a woman in labor. Verse 23 says believers groan too, 'waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.' So adoption is both now and not yet: already given, and still to be completed.

Heiser read Romans 8 as part of his family story. The sons of God being revealed, in his reading, is the human family stepping into its full place in God's household. Many Christian readers focus instead on the *resurrection* of the body and the renewal of creation. The two readings overlap: both see Romans 8 pointing to a future in which creation and God's children are made whole together.

words.d: legally taking someone into a family as a child with full rights; Paul's picture for becoming God's child
an Aramaic word for father, used by Jesus in Mark 14:36 and by Paul in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6
being raised to life in a renewed body; in Romans 8:23 Paul calls it the redemption of the body

look.title: Now and Not Yet
look.text: Romans 8:15 says believers have already received the Spirit of adoption. Romans 8:23 says they are still waiting for the adoption, the redemption of the body. Scholars often call this tension 'already and not yet': something given now and completed later.
look.prompt: Think of something in ordinary life that is already yours but not yet complete, like an acceptance letter before the first day. How does that help you explain Romans 8:15 and 8:23 together?

check.why: Abba is Aramaic for father; Paul keeps it inside his Greek letter in Romans 8:15.

check.q: In Romans 8:19, what is creation waiting for?
choices: The revealing of the sons of God
check.why: Romans 8:19 says creation waits for the manifestation, or revealing, of the sons of God.

check.q: What does Romans 8:23 connect with 'the adoption'?
check.why: Romans 8:23 says believers wait for the adoption, the redemption of the body.

lessons.title: Heirs in Galatians 4
lessons.mainIdea: Galatians 4:4–7 uses Roman-style adoption to say that believers are no longer slaves but sons and heirs of God.
reading: In Galatians 4:4–5 Paul writes that when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and under the law, so that 'we might receive the adoption of sons.' Verse 7 draws the result: 'thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an *heir* of God through Christ.' In the King James Version 'servant' translates the Greek word for slave. Paul's point is a change of status in a household.

Paul's readers knew *Roman adoption* well. A Roman adopted son took his new father's name, gained his rights and could inherit his estate. Old debts to his former family were set aside. The most famous case was Octavian, adopted in Julius Caesar's will, who became the emperor Augustus. So when Paul said believers were adopted, his audience heard a legal and permanent change: full sons, with a full share.

Heiser read Galatians 4 alongside Deuteronomy 32. The nations had been handed away to other powers. Now, through Christ, people from those nations could be adopted into God's own family and share his inheritance. Paul's Greek word for adoption, *huiothesia*, appears only in his letters. Other readers focus on Paul's argument about the law in Galatians: adoption shows that belonging to God comes through Christ, not through keeping the law of Moses.

words.d: a person who has the right to receive a parent's property or position
a legal act in Rome that made someone a full son, with the father's name, rights and inheritance
the Greek word for adoption as a son, used in the New Testament only by Paul

lessons.title: We Shall Judge Angels
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Corinthians 6:3 Paul tells believers they will judge angels, which Heiser read as a sign of their future place in God's council.
reading: In 1 Corinthians 6 Paul is upset that believers in Corinth are taking each other to court. He asks in verse 2 whether they know that the saints will judge the world. Then in verse 3 he asks, 'Know ye not that we shall judge angels?' His argument runs from larger to smaller: people who will judge angels should be able to settle ordinary disputes among themselves. Paul wrote this letter around 55 CE from Ephesus.

Paul does not explain the claim. He treats it as something his readers should already know. Heiser read the verse as a strong hint of his displacement idea. In the divine council, heavenly beings held roles of judgment and rule. If believers will judge angels, then they will stand in a place higher than those beings once held. Heiser linked this with Psalm 82, where God judges the gods who judged badly.

Readers take 'judge' in more than one way. Some say believers will share in Christ's final verdict on fallen angels, such as those mentioned in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6. Others read 'judge' as 'rule' or 'govern,' as the word sometimes means in the Hebrew Bible, where the judges were leaders. Some interpreters limit the angels to fallen ones, and others leave the question open. All agree the verse gives believers a surprising future role.

words.d: holy ones; in Paul's letters, a common name for all believers
to decide a case; in the Hebrew Bible it can also mean to lead or govern
heavenly beings who, in texts like 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6, sinned and are held for judgment

check.q: Which psalm did Heiser connect with 1 Corinthians 6:3?

check.q: Which is one other way readers take 'judge' in this verse?

lessons.title: Rule Over the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 2:26–27 and 3:21 promise the one who overcomes a share in Jesus's rule over the nations and a seat on his throne.
reading: Revelation 2–3 holds seven short letters to churches in Asia Minor, in what is now western Turkey. Each ends with a promise 'to him that overcometh.' The letter to Thyatira (Revelation 2:26–27) promises 'power over the nations' and borrows the words of Psalm 2:9: he will rule them with a rod of iron, and they will be broken like a potter's vessels. The letter to Laodicea (Revelation 3:21) promises a seat with Jesus on his throne.

Psalm 2 was a royal psalm. In it God tells his anointed king, 'Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance' (Psalm 2:8, KJV). The word 'heathen' there translates the Hebrew goyim, meaning nations. Revelation takes the promise made to the king and shares it with those who overcome. Heiser saw here the nations of Deuteronomy 32 finally coming back under God's rule, with Jesus and his people ruling where the fallen gods had ruled.

The picture of breaking pottery can sound harsh. Many commentators note that in the ancient world a shepherd's rod both guided and protected, and that Revelation's Greek verb in 2:27 can mean 'shepherd.' Others read the image as final justice against oppression. Interpreters also differ on when this rule happens: in a future reign on earth, in a heavenly reign now, or in both. The letters themselves stress faithfulness under pressure.

words.d: to win or stay faithful through hardship; the promises in Revelation 2–3 go 'to him that overcometh'
a Hebrew word for nations or peoples, often other than Israel
a psalm about Israel's king, such as Psalm 2 or Psalm 110

check.why: The rod of iron and the potter's vessels come from Psalm 2:9.

lessons.title: Jesus Quotes Psalm 82
lessons.mainIdea: In John 10:34–36 Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'Ye are gods,' and readers disagree about who those gods are and what his argument means.
reading: In John 10 a crowd in the temple courts accuses Jesus of blasphemy for making himself God. Jesus answers by quoting Psalm 82:6: 'Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?' (John 10:34). He goes on: if scripture called them gods 'unto whom the word of God came,' and scripture cannot be broken, why accuse him for saying 'I am the Son of God'? (John 10:35–36). The argument moves from the lesser case to the greater.

Readers identify the 'gods' in three main ways. Many Christian commentators, especially from the Reformation onward, read them as human judges who acted for God. Some rabbinic writings connect the verse with Israel at Sinai, when the people received the Torah. Heiser read Psalm 82 as a scene in the heavenly *divine council*, so the gods are real heavenly beings, the *elohim* who ruled the nations and failed.

Heiser argued that his reading still makes sense of John 10. In his view, Jesus points out that the scriptures themselves use elohim for beings other than the God of Israel, so the word alone cannot settle the charge. Critics of Heiser's reading ask why the phrase 'unto whom the word of God came' would fit heavenly beings. Heiser and others have offered answers, and the debate continues. Whatever the reading, Jesus's point stays the same: the crowd's charge does not fit their own scripture.

words.d: a Hebrew word that can mean God, gods or heavenly beings; Heiser called it a word for beings whose home is the unseen realm
the gathering of heavenly beings around God, which Heiser saw in Psalm 82
speech that dishonors God; the charge the crowd raises in John 10:33
an argument that if something holds in a smaller case, it holds even more in a larger one

lessons.title: Theosis in Eastern Orthodoxy
lessons.mainIdea: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach theosis, being united with God by grace, and they read it as sharing God's life, never becoming God by nature.
reading: In the early 300s CE, Athanasius, who became bishop of Alexandria in Egypt, wrote a short book called On the Incarnation. In one famous line he says, in a paraphrase, that God became human so that humans might become divine. Eastern Orthodox Christians use the word *theosis*, or deification, for this idea. They often pair it with 2 Peter 1:4, which speaks of becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' (KJV).

Orthodox teachers are careful about what theosis means. It is union with God by *grace*, a gift, not a change into God's own being. In the 1300s the monk and bishop Gregory Palamas described this with a distinction between God's essence, which no creature can share, and God's energies, his active presence, which humans can share. An iron in a fire is a common Orthodox picture: the iron glows with the fire's heat but remains iron.

Some readers notice that Heiser's family picture sounds close to theosis. Both speak of humans raised into a share of God's life and rule. Heiser's own emphasis was on the divine council and the story of the nations, not on the Orthodox language of energies. Western Christian traditions tend to use other words, such as glorification or sanctification, and some are cautious about the term theosis. Comparing them shows different traditions working on the same biblical passages.

words.d: an Eastern Orthodox teaching that humans are united with God and share his life by grace; also called deification
God's free gift, not earned; in theosis, the way humans share God's life
Gregory Palamas's distinction between God's being, which cannot be shared, and God's active presence, which can
the Christian teaching that the Son of God became a human being

lessons.title: Children of God in Jewish Readings
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew Bible calls Israel God's son and children, and Jewish tradition reads this as a covenant bond of love and duty, not as becoming divine.
reading: In Exodus 4:22 God sends a message to Pharaoh through Moses: 'Israel is my son, even my firstborn' (KJV). Deuteronomy 14:1 tells the people, 'Ye are the children of the LORD your God.' Hosea 11:1 remembers God calling his son out of Egypt. In these verses the whole people is God's child. The family language belongs to Israel long before the New Testament uses it.

Jewish tradition has usually read this family bond through the *covenant*, the binding agreement at Sinai. Being God's children brings closeness and also duty: to keep the commandments and to live as a holy people. A famous saying of Rabbi Akiva in the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot chapter 3, says that Israel is beloved because they are called children of God, and it was an extra sign of love that they were told so. The saying treats the title as love made known, not a change in nature.

Jewish readers generally do not describe people becoming divine, and the strong teaching of God's oneness in the *Shema* (Deuteronomy 6:4) shapes that. Christian readings like Heiser's build on the same Hebrew verses but apply the family language to all who trust in Jesus, from every nation. Comparing the readings shows where they share roots and where they part ways.

Deuteronomy 6:4, 'Hear, O Israel,' the central Jewish statement that God is one

lessons.title: Never Equal to God
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser insisted that however high believers are raised, they never become equal to God, who alone is uncreated and unique in kind.
reading: Heiser knew that talk of 'gods' and 'children of God' can be misheard. So he drew a firm line. In The Unseen Realm (2015) he argued that the word elohim names where a being lives, the unseen realm, not what rank it has. Many beings can be called elohim. But only the God of Israel is uncreated, all-powerful and worthy of worship. The other elohim were made by him. Heiser's point was that God is unique in kind, not just first among equals.

That line holds for believers too. In Heiser's reading, glorified humans will share God's council and rule, but they remain creatures. Readers who share this view often point to 1 John 3:2, which says believers will be 'like him,' meaning Jesus, when he appears. Being like someone is not the same as being him. The New Testament also says that Jesus is 'the firstborn among many brethren' (Romans 8:29): a family with an eldest, not a crowd of equals.

Other traditions draw the same line in their own words. Eastern Orthodoxy says humans share God's energies, never his essence. Jewish readings keep God's oneness at the center. Readers who disagree with Heiser about the divine council still agree with him here. Heiser's family picture, then, is about closeness and honor, not about humans turning into God.

the eldest child, with a place of honor; used of Jesus in Romans 8:29 and Colossians 1:15

chapters.title: Har Magedon and the New Eden
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Heiser read the last battle and the new Jerusalem of Revelation, and how do other readers of Revelation see them?

story.title: The Hill with Cities Inside
story.kicker: On a school trip to Israel, a group stands on the mound of Megiddo and asks where the famous mountain of Armageddon is.
paragraphs: The bus climbed a low road and stopped at the edge of a wide green valley. The tour guide, a patient archaeologist named Dalia, led the students up a path to the top of a flat-topped mound. Below them the Jezreel Valley stretched out in fields of wheat and sunflowers. 'This is Tel Megiddo,' she said. 'A tel is a hill made by people. Every city here was built on top of the ruins of the one before.'

She pointed to a deep trench cut by excavators. In its walls the students could see bands of stone, ash and packed earth, one above another. 'Archaeologists count more than twenty layers of cities here,' Dalia said, 'from long before Israel's kings down to Persian times.' The city guarded an old road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Pharaoh Thutmose III fought a battle here in the 1400s BCE, and 2 Kings 23:29 says King Josiah of Judah died here in 609 BCE.

A student named Marcus raised his hand. 'My grandmother says the last battle happens at Armageddon. Is this it?' Dalia smiled. 'The book of Revelation says the kings gather at a place called in Hebrew Armageddon, or Har Magedon. Har means mountain. Many readers take it to mean the mountain of Megiddo.' Marcus looked around at the gentle mound. 'This is not much of a mountain,' he said.

'You are not the first to notice,' Dalia said. 'Some scholars think the name points somewhere else.' She told them about Michael Heiser, a scholar of Hebrew who read Har Magedon as an echo of a different phrase in Isaiah, the mountain of assembly, where God's council meets. Other readers see the name as a symbol, drawn from Megiddo's long story of battles.

On the bus home Marcus opened Revelation on his phone. He read past the battle to the last two chapters: a city with a river and a tree, and nations walking in its light. He wrote a note to himself: the book does not end with a battle. It ends with a garden city.
story.think: Why might a name in Revelation carry a hidden meaning from the Hebrew Bible? What would you need to check before trusting such a reading?

lessons.title: One Verse, One Name
lessons.mainIdea: The name Armageddon appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 16:16, as a Greek spelling of a Hebrew place name.
reading: Revelation is the last book of the Christian Bible. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:9). Many scholars date it to around 95 CE, and some date it earlier, near 68 CE. Chapters 15 and 16 describe seven angels pouring out seven *bowls* of judgment. Between the sixth and seventh bowls comes a short scene about a gathering for battle.

In Revelation 16:13–14 John sees three unclean spirits like frogs come from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. They go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for 'the battle of that great day of God Almighty.' Then verse 16 names the place: 'a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon.' In the Greek of the earliest manuscripts the name is spelled *Harmagedon*. That is the only place the name appears in the whole Bible.

John does not describe the battle in chapter 16. The seventh bowl follows at once, and the battle itself is told later, briefly, in Revelation 19:11–21. Because the name appears only once, readers must work out its meaning from its Hebrew parts. John's words 'in the Hebrew tongue' invite exactly that. The next lessons look at how readers have done it.

words.d: the last book of the New Testament, a book of visions given to John on Patmos
in Revelation 15–16, the seven bowls of judgment poured out by seven angels
the Greek spelling of the place name in Revelation 16:16, usually written Armageddon in English

lessons.title: The Usual Reading: Megiddo
lessons.mainIdea: Most readers take Har Magedon to mean 'mountain of Megiddo,' a city in northern Israel with a long history of battles.
reading: In Hebrew, *har* means mountain or hill. The second part, Magedon, looks like Megiddo, a city at the edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel. So the most common reading is 'mountain of Megiddo.' Megiddo is a *tel*, a mound built up from many layers of ruined cities. Archaeologists count more than twenty of them. It became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.

Megiddo guarded a pass on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, so armies met there again and again. Pharaoh Thutmose III won a famous battle there in the 1400s BCE, recorded on the walls of the temple at Karnak. Judges 5:19 sets a battle 'by the waters of Megiddo.' 2 Kings 23:29 says King Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BCE facing Pharaoh Necho. In 1918 the British general Edmund Allenby fought a battle nearby that took the name Megiddo.

For many readers, that history is the point. John chose a place whose name already meant war, the way a person today might say 'Waterloo' for a final defeat. Futurist readers often expect armies to gather in the Jezreel Valley itself. Symbolic readers see Megiddo as a picture of every final clash between good and evil. Both start from the place name.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning mountain or hill
a mound formed by layers of ruined towns built one on top of another
a broad, fertile valley in northern Israel, overlooked by Megiddo

lessons.title: A Mountain Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Megiddo is a mound on a plain, and no Hebrew Bible text speaks of a Mount Megiddo, which leads some scholars to look for another meaning.
reading: Marcus's comment on the bus trip points to a real problem. Megiddo sits on a mound that rises only modestly above the valley. It is not a mountain in any ordinary sense. The Hebrew Bible speaks of the city of Megiddo, the waters of Megiddo, and the valley or plain of Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:22; Zechariah 12:11). It never speaks of a 'mountain of Megiddo.'

Scholars have answered this in different ways. Some say John meant the hills near Megiddo, such as Mount Carmel a few miles to the northwest. Some say the tel itself, after so many cities, was hill enough. Others say the name is symbolic, so it need not match any map. A few scholars, long before Heiser, suggested that Har Magedon was a different Hebrew phrase that later readers had mistaken for Megiddo.

This is how careful reading works. A reader notices a detail that does not fit, then asks what would explain it. The answer may be simple or may need more digging. Heiser took the mountain problem seriously, and it led him back to the Hebrew Bible's language of God's mountain. His answer is the subject of the next section.

words.d: a ridge of hills in northern Israel near Megiddo, where 1 Kings 18 sets Elijah's contest
standing for an idea rather than for a literal thing or place
the flat land around Megiddo, named in 2 Chronicles 35:22 and Zechariah 12:11

look.title: What the Map Says

lessons.title: The Mount of Assembly in Isaiah 14
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 14:13 speaks of har mo'ed, the 'mount of assembly,' the high meeting place of God's council, which a rebel boasts he will climb.
reading: Isaiah 14 is a taunt song against the king of Babylon. In verses 12–15 it turns to a bright figure, called in Hebrew Helel ben Shahar, 'shining one, son of the dawn,' who has fallen from heaven. In verse 13 this figure boasts that he will raise his throne above the stars of God and sit on 'the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north' (KJV). The Hebrew for 'mount of the congregation' is *har mo'ed*, often translated 'mount of assembly.'

Mo'ed means an appointed meeting or assembly. The same word appears in the tent of meeting, where God met Moses. Heiser read har mo'ed as the mountain where God's *divine council* gathers. The phrase 'sides of the north' translates the Hebrew *Zaphon*, the name of a mountain where, in texts from Ugarit, the god Baal had his palace. Psalm 48:2 uses the same word for Mount Zion, calling it beautiful 'on the sides of the north.'

Heiser read Isaiah 14 as a double picture: a human king and, behind him, a heavenly rebel who tried to seize the council's mountain. Many interpreters read verses 12–15 only as poetry about the king of Babylon's pride. Christian tradition has often connected the shining one with Satan; the Latin Vulgate's word Lucifer comes from here. Either way, the verse gives a name, har mo'ed, for the mountain where God's council meets.

words.d: Hebrew for 'mount of assembly,' the council's mountain named in Isaiah 14:13
Hebrew for 'north'; also a mountain linked with Baal at Ugarit and used of Mount Zion in Psalm 48:2
the gathering of heavenly beings around God's throne
a poem that mocks a fallen enemy, like Isaiah 14 against the king of Babylon

lessons.title: From Mo'ed to Magedon
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the Greek Harmagedon can come from Hebrew har mo'ed, because Greek often wrote the Hebrew letter ayin with a g sound.
reading: How could har mo'ed become Harmagedon? Heiser's answer, building on earlier scholars, rests on one Hebrew letter. Mo'ed begins with m and then has the letter *ayin*, a throat sound that Greek has no letter for. When Greek writers spelled Hebrew names, they sometimes wrote ayin as a g. The city Hebrew calls 'Amorah became Gomorrah. The city Hebrew calls 'Azzah became Gaza. Both g sounds stand for ayin.

So a Hebrew phrase like har mo'ed, spelled in Greek letters, could come out close to har-mog-ed, and with a common ending, Harmagedon. Heiser argued that John, who says the name is 'in the Hebrew tongue,' was pointing readers to the mount of assembly. If so, the last battle is not about a hill in the Jezreel Valley. It is about God's own mountain, the place where his council meets, which the Hebrew Bible also calls Zion.

Scholars weigh this carefully. Supporters note that it solves the mountain problem and fits Revelation's many echoes of Isaiah. Critics note that the spelling match is not exact and that Megiddo remains the simpler explanation of the Greek. Heiser presented it in The Unseen Realm (2015) as the reading that best fit the Bible's theme of the cosmic mountain. Like much in Revelation, it remains debated, and good readers can hold it as one serious option.

words.d: a letter of the Hebrew alphabet with a throat sound that Greek had no letter for
writing a word from one language in the letters of another, like Hebrew names in Greek
the idea, common in the ancient Near East, of a holy mountain where heaven and earth meet and the gods meet

look.title: Following One Letter
look.text: Hebrew 'Amorah (with ayin) became Greek Gomorrha. Hebrew 'Azzah (with ayin) became Greek Gaza. Hebrew har mo'ed (with ayin after the m) could become Greek Har-mag-ed. Heiser read Harmagedon this way. Many other scholars read it as Har + Megiddo.

check.why: Greek sometimes wrote ayin as g, as in Gomorrah and Gaza.

lessons.title: The Powers' Last Stand
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the battle of Revelation 16 and 19–20 as the rebel powers' final attack on God's mountain, Zion, where his council meets.
reading: In Heiser's reading, the gathering at Har Magedon is not a war over land or oil. It is the last move of the powers who have ruled the nations since Babel. In Revelation 16:13–14 unclean spirits gather the kings of the world. Heiser read this as the fallen gods of the nations rallying their peoples one last time, against the mountain where God rules, the place the rebel of Isaiah 14 wanted to take.

He pointed to Hebrew Bible texts that set the final battle at Jerusalem. Zechariah 14:2 says God will gather all nations against Jerusalem. Joel 3:2 speaks of gathering the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat. Revelation 20:9 says the nations surround 'the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city.' Heiser saw a contrast with Mount *Hermon*, where 1 Enoch 6 says the Watchers came down to begin their rebellion. The story that began on one mountain ends on another.

Revelation describes this battle briefly and without suspense. In 19:11–21 a rider called Faithful and True wins by the sword from his mouth, which many readers take to mean his word. In 20:9 fire comes down, and it is over. Futurist readers often expect a literal gathering of armies. Idealist readers see a picture of the end of all evil. Heiser's reading adds the divine council background without deciding every detail of timing.

words.d: a high mountain north of Israel; 1 Enoch 6 says the Watchers descended there
the hill of Jerusalem, often used in the Bible for God's holy mountain and dwelling
a final fight by a side that is about to lose

lessons.title: The Dragon Bound
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 20 tells of Satan bound for a thousand years and then removed for good, and readers hold three main views of that thousand years.
reading: Revelation 20:1–3 describes an angel coming down with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain. He seizes the dragon, whom the text names 'that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan,' and binds him for a thousand years so he cannot deceive the nations. After that, verses 7–10 say, he is released briefly, gathers the nations one last time, and is thrown into the lake of fire. The scene is short, and the text treats his defeat as certain.

Heiser noticed the words 'old serpent.' They point back to the serpent of Eden, the *nachash* of Genesis 3. In his reading, the being who first disrupted God's family in the garden is finally removed before the garden is restored in Revelation 21–22. He also noticed the phrase 'deceive the nations,' which fits his reading of the nations handed to other powers after Babel.

The thousand years is called the *millennium*, from Latin for a thousand years. Premillennial readers expect Jesus to return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Postmillennial readers expect the reign to come gradually before his return. Amillennial readers take the thousand years as a symbol of the present age. Christians have held all three views for centuries. Revelation 20 is the only passage that names the thousand years.

words.d: the Hebrew word for the serpent in Genesis 3; Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 call the dragon 'that old serpent'
the thousand years of Revelation 20, from the Latin for a thousand years
the view that Jesus returns before a literal thousand-year reign
the view that the thousand years is a symbol of the present age

lessons.title: A City Shaped Like a Cube
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 21:16 describes the new Jerusalem as equal in length, width and height, like the cube-shaped holy of holies in Solomon's temple.
reading: In Revelation 21 John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' and the new Jerusalem coming down from God. An angel measures the city with a golden reed. Revelation 21:16 says the city 'lieth foursquare' and that its length, breadth and height are equal: twelve thousand furlongs, or *stadia*, each way. That is roughly 1,400 miles. The shape is a cube, or possibly a pyramid, though most readers take it as a cube.

The Hebrew Bible has one famous cube. 1 Kings 6:20 says the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, the *holy of holies*, was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high. That room held the ark of the covenant and was where God's presence was said to dwell. Only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). John's city takes the holy of holies' shape and makes it the size of a whole world.

Revelation 21:22 then says John saw no temple in the city, because God and the Lamb are its temple. Revelation 21:3 says the dwelling of God is with humans. Heiser read this as the goal of the whole story: God's presence, once limited to one room, now fills the place where his family lives. Many readers across traditions agree the cube points to the holy of holies, even when they read the numbers symbolically.

words.d: the innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, where God's presence was said to dwell

lessons.title: A Garden in the City
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 22:1–3 fills the city with a river and the tree of life, and Heiser read it as Eden restored.
reading: Revelation 22 opens with a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. On either side of the river stands the *tree of life*, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month. Verse 3 says there will be no more curse. Each of these details echoes Genesis 2–3, where a river flows out of Eden (Genesis 2:10), the tree of life grows in the garden (2:9), and the curse follows the first rebellion (3:14–19).

Heiser read Eden not only as a garden but as God's home on a holy mountain, where his council met. He pointed to Ezekiel 28:13–14, which calls Eden 'the garden of God' and speaks of 'the holy mountain of God.' In his reading, Revelation 21–22 brings all three together: the mountain, the garden and the holy city. The story that began in a garden ends in a garden city, with God dwelling among his family.

Ezekiel 47 gives a close parallel: a river flows from the temple and trees grow along its banks, with fruit every month and leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). Many scholars see John drawing on Ezekiel. Readers differ on whether Revelation 22 describes a literal renewed earth, a heavenly reality, or a picture of life with God. They widely agree that its images come from Eden, from Ezekiel, and from the temple.

words.d: the tree in Eden (Genesis 2:9) that returns in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2)

lessons.title: Healing for the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 21–22 shows the nations walking in the city's light and healed by the tree's leaves, which Heiser read as the nations reclaimed after Babel.
reading: Revelation 22:2 says the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations.' Revelation 21:24 says the nations will walk in the city's light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Verse 25 says its gates will never be shut. Earlier, Revelation 7:9 describes a crowd from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne.

Heiser read these verses as the ending of the Babel story. At Babel the nations were scattered and handed to other powers (Genesis 11; Deuteronomy 32:8). Throughout the Hebrew Bible, prophets hoped they would come back: Isaiah 2:2–3 pictures many peoples streaming to the mountain of the LORD's house. In Revelation, the rulers who led the nations astray are gone, and the nations come to God's mountain city in peace. The *disinherited nations* are welcomed home.

Other readers agree that Revelation borrows Isaiah's hope for the nations, and they stress different parts. Some focus on the church drawn from every people. Some focus on the renewal of whole cultures, their 'glory and honor' brought in. Some read the scene as a picture of a healed humanity. Across readings, the city's twelve gates, open on every side, picture a welcome rather than a wall.

lessons.title: Four Approaches
lessons.mainIdea: Readers approach Revelation in four main ways, preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist, and many combine them.
reading: Revelation has been read in many ways, and scholars usually group them into four approaches. A *preterist* reading, from Latin for past, holds that most of the book describes events of John's own time, such as Rome's persecution of Christians or the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. A *historicist* reading holds that the book maps out church history from John's day to the end. Many Protestant Reformers read it this way.

A *futurist* reading holds that most of the book, from chapter 4 onward, describes events still to come before the end. This view is widespread among evangelical Christians in the United States today. An *idealist* reading holds that the book pictures timeless truths, the struggle of good and evil and God's final victory, rather than particular events. Each approach can point to features of the text that support it.

Many modern scholars mix approaches. They read Revelation first as a letter to seven real churches in the first century (Revelation 1:4), then ask what it hoped for beyond that. Heiser's contribution is less about which approach to choose and more about the Hebrew Bible background that any approach can use: the divine council, the nations, the cosmic mountain and Eden. His readings of Har Magedon and the new Jerusalem can fit more than one of the four.

words.d: reading Revelation as mostly about events of John's own time

lessons.title: Reading Revelation Calmly
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation is written in symbols drawn from the Hebrew Bible, and careful readers check claims against the text rather than headlines.
reading: Revelation uses numbers as patterns. There are seven letters, seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls. Twelve returns in the gates, the foundations and the tree's fruit. Many scholars read seven as completeness and twelve as God's people, from Israel's twelve tribes. This is not a code to be cracked with dates. It is a way of writing called *apocalyptic*, full of symbols, that many Jewish books of the time also used, such as Daniel and 1 Enoch.

Over the centuries, many people have announced that Revelation's battles were about to happen in their own day, naming leaders and dates. Those predictions have not come true. Heiser was openly critical of sensational claims about the Bible. He asked readers to start with what the words meant to their first readers, in the Hebrew Bible and the ancient world. That is how he came to Har Magedon and the mount of assembly.

A careful reader can ask three questions of any claim about Revelation. What does the text actually say, in which verse? What Hebrew Bible passage does it echo? Who holds this reading, and who reads it differently? The book itself ends not with fear but with an invitation, 'Come' (Revelation 22:17), and with God wiping away tears (Revelation 21:4). Readers of every approach notice that ending.

words.d: a kind of ancient writing that reveals hidden realities through visions and symbols, as in Daniel, 1 Enoch and Revelation
an image or number that stands for an idea, such as seven for completeness
presented to shock or excite rather than to inform
